title: What we know after local police say ICE mistakenly detained US citizen | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Days after local police said Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained a US citizen in Evanston, Illinois, and left him injured on the ground, questions are swirling about what happened during the targeted enforcement operation gone awry — and the circumstances under which federal immigration officers can detain people.

The Evanston Police Department said the man, whom police have identified only as an Evanston resident, resembled someone federal agents were seeking. The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement the man “was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself.”

The man was later released, local police said, after agents determined he was not the person they were looking for and learned he was a US citizen.

At the time of Sunday’s incident, five federal agents were operating in separate vehicles as they searched the area for their target, one agent told an Evanston officer.

The incident is the latest instance of aUS citizen caught upin the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, which has featured highly visible enforcement operations and aggressive tactics that have prompted nationwide protests, legal battles and political backlash.

Here’s what we know so far aboutthe incident.

Around 9:49 a.m. on September 20, Evanston officers were called to the area after receiving reports of two men arguing, police said in a statement. When officers arrived, they found the man on the ground with several bystanders helping him, police said.

Officials called an ambulance after the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth. Witnesses told officers they believed ICE agents were attempting to detain him, according to police.

While responding to the scene in Evanston, a suburb of Chicago, one officer encountered two SUVs near an intersection and spoke with an individual in one of the vehicles, who identified himself as a federal agent conducting a “fugitive investigation,” police said. The person was dressed in plain clothes and wearing a vest marked “POLICE” with federal law enforcement markings, according to police.

A DHS spokesperson told CNN, “ICE encountered an individual who resembled the target. ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement,” but said the man did not identify himself.

The ICE agents “later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the statement continued.

Evanston police said they are continuing to investigate the incident, and officers are preserving available body camera footage and interviewing witnesses.

Evanston’s police chief met with the man at a local hospital, and an evidence technician photographed and documented his injuries. Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss said in a statement on X that the wrongfully detained man wastreated for minor injuries atSaint Francis Hospital.

DHS said the man refused assistance from ICE agents — but did not address the man’s injuries in its statement.

Evanston police said its officer reported seeing blood on the hands of the agent in the SUV, which the federal official said resulted from an injury he received while trying to detain the man. The agent declined medical treatment.

No further information is known about the man whom officials say was mistakenly detained or the agents involved.

Surveillance video obtained by CNN provides another perspective of the encounter, which appears to show two agents and the man in an upright struggle before federal officials take him to the ground.

As the confrontation draws the attention of several people nearby, at least three drivers pull into the nearby parking lot and exit their vehicles, joining other bystanders, some recording.

Cellphone video recorded by a witness, which begins as the confrontation is already underway, shows the man being held on the ground.

Two agents are seen standing behind a black SUV, with one appearing to hold the man down, in the video CNN obtained.

A man’s voice is heard saying, “I’m a f**king US citizen.” The officers, one of whomismasked and wearing a hood, then appear to release him and step away.

The man can be heard telling the officers not to touch him as they move away from him.

Moments after releasing the man, the two agents return to their vehicles and leave the scene, while the man continues to lie face down on the ground in the street. A man wearing a cap kneels beside the man, gently placing a hand on his back and appearing to call for help. Several other people can also be heard trying to assist him.

One witness, Miguel Olivares, toldCNN affiliate WLShe was taking a break while helping out at a nearby Mexican restaurant when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.

“It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, ‘I’m a US citizen. I’m a US citizen,’” Olivares said, at which point he began filming.

“They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face,” Olivares said. He and others tried to comfort the man after agents released him.

Ryan Garton, the man seen wearing a cap and appearing to call for help, says he was headed home from one of his son’s sports activities when he drove past the scene.

“I saw two people who looked like ICE agents,” he told CNN Thursday. “They were punching a guy and putting their knee into his back.”

“I then just immediately pulled my car to the side of the road and was like, ‘No, I’m not going to let this happen,’” Garton recalled. He says he crossed the street and confronted the ICE agents, telling them to back off and that he would administer first aid.

The agents, Garton says, did not offer the man assistance before heading to their vehicles and leaving the scene. The man had screamed, “Get away from me! Don’t touch me! Don’t touch me!” at the agents, Garton said, adding, “What else was he supposed to say?”

After the agents left, Garton said he tried to reassure the man. “I kneeled down at the victim’s head and put my hand on his back and said, ‘I have you. You’re safe. They can’t hurt you anymore.’ And then proceeded to just stay there with him,” Garton said.

The man himself, he said, had dialed 911 but was in shock and unable to speak to dispatchers, so Garton took the phone and relayed to Evanston dispatch their location, the license plates and descriptions of the ICE agents, and paramedic support was likely needed.

The man had facial abrasions, a “clearly swollen” right temple and blood coming from his mouth, Garton said. He also noted bloody knuckle prints on the back, side and front of the man’s clothing.

The man told Garton that he had been in the emergency room the day before and was headed to the pharmacy to pick up a prescription when the agents targeted him.

The man repeatedly asked, “Why are they attacking me? I’m a citizen. Why are they attacking me?” Garton recalled.

Garton said he gave several official statements and identified for police the ICE agent he saw punch the man.

In response to a CNN request for comment, a DHS spokesperson said, “ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.”

Kate Huddleston, a senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union Immigrants’ Rights Project, told CNN that under the statute, ICE has limited authority to make civil immigration arrests — with two qualifications.

Agents must first have probable cause to both believe a person is undocumented and the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, she said.

Huddleston explained that, for agents to have probable cause to believe a person is likely to escape, they must have reason to believe the individual could not be found in the future, which could include having few ties to the community, no family members in the area or no permanent place of employment where the person could be located.

“For a person who’s merely walking down the street or driving in a car, whom ICE happens to see, there’s not necessarily anything about an individual whom they encounter in the community that would give rise to reasonable suspicion, absent someone affirmatively stating something like ‘I’m undocumented,’ or ICE having some sort of evidence that that individual is undocumented,” she said.

Huddleston added that a person who is detained in violation of the Constitution can seek relief, including under theFederal Tort Claims Act,which allows individuals who have been injured by the “wrongful or negligent act” of a federal employee to file a claim for reimbursement.

DHS said its “enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.”

“We know who we are targeting ahead of time,” the agency said. “If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability.”
